scenarios.title: The room that holds its temperature
scenarios.situation: A facilities team installs a heater that runs at full power whenever the room is below target and shuts off above target. The room swings between chilly and stifling, and the team blames the heater's wattage.
scenarios.prompt: What is actually wrong, in cybernetic terms?
evidence: Feedback

A negative feedback loop senses the output (temperature) and acts to reduce the deviation from the goal. The heater already implements one — the problem is not missing feedback but its crude form: full-on/full-off control with no modulation overshoots the target in both directions.
choices: The loop exists but is badly tuned: bang-bang control with no proportional response overshoots, so the fix is better control (e.g., proportional or PID control), not a bigger heater.
The system has positive feedback: the heater amplifies temperature errors, and the only fix is to remove the sensor.
The system has no feedback at all; a thermostat cannot work without a digital computer.
The wattage is simply too high; a smaller heater would hold temperature steady without any control changes.
scenarios.why: Negative feedback is present — the sensor does drive the heater. The failure is in the control law: on/off switching around the setpoint guarantees oscillation. Cybernetics distinguishes the loop's existence from its tuning.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem that feedback is missing, or that it is crude?
objectives: negative feedback
control

scenarios.title: Which way does the loop go?
scenarios.situation: During a market panic, falling prices frighten investors, who sell, which pushes prices lower. A commentator calls this 'the market's thermostat restoring balance.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the thermostat analogy?
choices: The loop is positive, not negative: falling prices cause more selling, which amplifies the fall — the opposite of a thermostat, which counteracts deviation. The commentator has the sign of the feedback backwards.
The analogy is correct: markets always return to equilibrium, exactly like a thermostat.
The analogy fails because markets have no sensors; feedback requires electronic measurement.
The analogy fails because thermostats cannot model human behavior under any circumstances.
scenarios.why: Sign matters more than the word 'feedback'. Negative feedback damps deviation toward a goal; positive feedback amplifies it away from the goal. Panics are runaway positive loops.
scenarios.hint: Does the effect oppose the cause, or reinforce it?
objectives: positive vs negative feedback

scenarios.title: The wobbling shower
scenarios.situation: An engineer models an office HVAC controller that reads the room sensor, but the sensor data arrives 10 minutes late. In simulation the temperature oscillates wildly even though the control law is a textbook negative-feedback design.
scenarios.prompt: What explains the oscillation?
evidence: Delay destabilizes feedback

Wiener and the early control engineers learned that delay in a feedback loop turns correction into overcorrection: by the time the sensor reports 'too cold,' the heater has already been running too long. Sufficient delay makes even negative feedback oscillate or diverge.
choices: Sensor delay: the controller acts on stale information, so its corrections arrive out of phase and overshoot — a stable control law becomes oscillatory once the loop delay exceeds the system's response time.
The control law must be positive feedback in disguise; negative feedback can never oscillate.
The simulation timestep is too coarse; real hardware would not oscillate.
The sensor is miscalibrated; recalibration alone will remove the oscillation regardless of delay.
scenarios.why: Feedback acts on the past. When delay is large relative to how fast the system responds, yesterday's correction becomes today's overshoot. This is why control design starts with loop timing, not just the control law.
scenarios.hint: What does the controller know, and when does it know it?
objectives: feedback delay
stability

scenarios.title: The regulator's variety
scenarios.situation: A data-center team builds an automated controller to keep 5,000 servers within thermal limits during heat waves, cold snaps, hardware failures, and traffic spikes. The controller handles exactly one scenario: 'it is hot outside.' The first cold snap crashes the cooling plant.
scenarios.prompt: Which cybernetic principle did the design violate?
evidence: Ashby's law of requisite variety

W. Ross Ashby's law states that a regulator must have at least as much variety (distinct responses) as the disturbances it regulates — 'only variety can destroy variety.' A one-response controller cannot regulate a many-disturbance environment.
choices: Requisite variety: the controller's repertoire (one response) is smaller than the disturbance set (heat, cold, failure, spikes), so unmodeled disturbances defeat it — the fix is widening the controller's variety, not tuning the single response.
The law of unintended consequences: automation always fails, so the plant should be run manually.
Occam's razor: the controller should be even simpler, with zero responses and a fixed schedule.
Moore's law: the controller needs faster hardware to handle the cold snap.
scenarios.why: Control is a matching problem: the regulator's variety must cover the environment's variety. Every disturbance you cannot respond to is a disturbance that controls you.
scenarios.hint: Count the disturbances, then count the responses. What must be true?
objectives: Ashby
requisite variety

scenarios.title: The observer in the loop
scenarios.situation: A company evaluates its new AI support agent by having the agent's own training team write the test questions, run the evaluation, and publish the score. The score is excellent; customers disagree.
scenarios.prompt: What does second-order cybernetics say about this evaluation?
evidence: Second-order cybernetics

Heinz von Foerster and the later cyberneticians insisted the observer is part of the system: who measures, with what interests and instruments, shapes what is observed. An evaluation cannot be understood apart from the evaluator's position in the loop.
choices: The evaluation is compromised at the design level: the observers (the training team) are inside the system they measure, with an interest in a good score — second-order cybernetics requires accounting for the observer, e.g., independent evaluators and customer-grounded metrics.
The evaluation is fine; second-order cybernetics proves that self-evaluation is the most accurate method.
The problem is sample size; the same team running more questions would fix the disagreement.
Observer effects apply only to quantum physics, not to software evaluation.
scenarios.why: First-order cybernetics studies the observed system; second-order studies the observing system. When the measurer benefits from the measurement, the loop includes the incentive — design the evaluation for that.
scenarios.hint: Who is watching the watcher, and what do they gain?
objectives: second-order cybernetics
evaluation

scenarios.title: The cost of surprise
scenarios.situation: Two logging formats record the same events. Format A uses a fixed 8-bit code per event type; Format B uses short codes for common events and long codes for rare ones. A teammate claims Format A is 'more efficient because every code is the same size.'
scenarios.prompt: Which format is more efficient, and what principle decides it?
evidence: Shannon entropy (1948)

Claude Shannon's 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' defined information entropy: the average surprise of a message source. Optimal codes give frequent symbols short codes — the average length cannot go below the entropy, and variable-length coding approaches it. Uniform codes waste bits on predictable symbols.
choices: Format B: Shannon's source coding theorem shows the lower bound on average code length is the entropy of the source, achieved by assigning shorter codes to more probable events — fixed-length codes overpay for predictable events.
Format A: uniform codes are always optimal because they simplify decoding, regardless of event probabilities.
They are equally efficient: both record the same events, so information content is identical.
Format A: entropy measures disorder, and uniform codes minimize disorder.
scenarios.why: Efficiency is about the average, not the individual code: match code length to probability. That is the operational meaning of entropy — expected surprise — and the basis of all modern compression.
scenarios.hint: If some events are far more common, where should the bits go?
objectives: Shannon entropy
coding

scenarios.title: The Black Box on the Factory Floor
scenarios.situation: A packaging machine on your factory line misbehaves intermittently: sometimes it seals cartons, sometimes it crushes them. The vendor manual is lost and the machine's internals are sealed. You can vary the input settings (belt speed, temperature, carton size) and observe the outputs (seal quality, crush rate). Your manager wants the housing cut open for inspection.
scenarios.prompt: Applying the cybernetic black-box method, what is your best first move?
choices: Systematically vary one input at a time, record input-output pairs, and build a model of the machine's behavior without opening it
Cut the housing open immediately, since only the internal mechanism explains the fault
Replace the machine, because intermittent faults in sealed systems cannot be diagnosed
Increase belt speed to maximum to force the fault to appear continuously, then inspect
scenarios.why: The black-box method treats the system by its observable input-output relations: controlled variation of inputs plus careful recording of outputs lets you infer the transfer behavior and isolate the fault condition without destroying the system. Opening it first risks changing the very behavior you need to explain.
scenarios.hint: Ashby's black box: you learn a system by what goes in and what comes out, not by assuming you must see inside.
objectives: Apply the black-box method to an unknown system
Distinguish behavioral modeling from structural inspection
evidence: Describes a controlled input-variation experiment with recorded outputs

scenarios.title: Requisite Variety in the Control Room
scenarios.situation: You supervise a regional power-grid control desk. Disturbances arrive in 12 distinct types (line faults, demand spikes, generator trips, and so on). Your control team currently has 5 standard response procedures. Last quarter, three novel disturbance combinations cascaded into outages because no procedure matched them.
scenarios.prompt: Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety says only variety can destroy variety. What does it prescribe here?
choices: Reduce the variety of disturbances by disconnecting volatile grid segments, since the regulator cannot match them
Increase the regulator's variety: add response procedures, cross-train operators, and build adaptive playbooks until control variety matches disturbance variety
Automate the 5 existing procedures so they execute faster; speed compensates for missing variety
Centralize all decisions with the shift supervisor to eliminate inconsistent responses
scenarios.why: Requisite variety demands the controller's repertoire be at least as rich as the disturbances it must absorb. Faster execution of 5 procedures cannot handle a 12-type disturbance space; only expanding control variety (more procedures, trained judgment, adaptive playbooks) closes the gap.
scenarios.hint: Count the varieties: 12 disturbance types vs 5 responses. Which side must grow?
objectives: State Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety
Apply it to a control-system staffing decision
evidence: Identifies the variety gap (12 vs 5) and prescribes expanding regulator variety

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Cybernetics as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Cybernetics Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Cybernetics is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Cybernetics?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Cybernetics issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Cybernetics is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Cybernetics supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Cybernetics failure in Cybernetics.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Cybernetics
Trace failures through layered dependencies
Distinguish symptoms from root causes
evidence: System Status
All Cybernetics components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a Thermostat
scenarios.situation: A homeowner complains the house swings between chilly and stuffy even though the thermostat is set to 70F. You inspect: the thermostat sensor sits directly above a heat vent, the furnace is oversized for the house, and the thermostat has no anticipator adjustment. The owner asks which single part to replace.
scenarios.prompt: Reading the thermostat as a sensor-comparator-effector loop, where is the structural fault?
choices: The sensor placement: sitting above the vent, it samples hot air instead of room air, so the comparator acts on false feedback
The furnace: oversizing means it heats too fast, so replace it with a smaller unit
The setpoint dial: 70F is simply the wrong target for this house
The homeowner's expectations: some swing is normal and no fix is needed
scenarios.why: In loop anatomy, the sensor feeds the comparator; a sensor sampling the wrong variable (vent air, not room air) corrupts every downstream decision, producing oscillation. Relocating the sensor repairs the feedback path itself, which is the structural fault — the furnace size is secondary.
scenarios.hint: Trace the loop: sensor -> comparator -> effector. Which link is lying?
objectives: Decompose a control loop into sensor, comparator, and effector
Diagnose oscillation from sensor placement
evidence: Names the sensor-comparator-effector chain and locates the fault at the sensor

scenarios.title: Anatomy of Homeostasis
scenarios.situation: During a winter hike, a companion starts shivering violently, then the shivering stops even though the cold continues. An hour later they become confused and drowsy. A fellow hiker says the stopped shivering means the body has adapted and they are fine now.
scenarios.prompt: As a homeostatic feedback system, what does the stopped shivering actually signal?
choices: Successful adaptation: the setpoint has shifted and the body no longer needs to generate heat
Effector exhaustion: the shivering mechanism (heat production) has failed while the disturbance continues, so core temperature is now falling unchecked
Sensor failure: the skin thermoreceptors have gone numb, which is harmless on its own
A secondary loop taking over: sweating will begin to compensate for the cold
scenarios.why: Shivering is the effector in the thermoregulatory loop; when it ceases while the cold disturbance persists, the loop has lost its corrective arm, not reached its goal. Confusion and drowsiness confirm core temperature is dropping — a loop failure, not adaptation. This is a medical emergency pattern.
scenarios.hint: An effector that quits while the disturbance continues is loop failure, not success.
objectives: Map physiological regulation onto feedback-loop anatomy
Distinguish loop success from effector failure
evidence: Identifies shivering as the effector and its cessation as loop failure

scenarios.title: Anatomy of a PID Controller
scenarios.situation: Your team's delivery drone oscillates in altitude: it climbs past the target, dives below it, climbs again. The flight controller is a PID loop. Telemetry shows the oscillation period is steady and the amplitude is not decaying. A teammate proposes cranking up the proportional gain to force it onto target faster.
scenarios.prompt: Reading the PID anatomy, what is the disciplined diagnosis and first tuning move?
choices: Increase proportional gain: stronger correction always reduces steady oscillation
The loop is underdamped and oscillating; increase derivative gain (damping) first, and re-check integral windup, before touching proportional gain
Disable the integral term permanently: integrators cause all oscillation
Add a feedforward term and ignore the oscillation: feedforward overrides feedback problems
scenarios.why: Steady, non-decaying oscillation is the signature of an underdamped loop with insufficient derivative (damping) action; more proportional gain typically worsens it. The disciplined move is to add damping first, then verify the integrator is not wound up, keeping the P-I-D anatomy balanced.
scenarios.hint: P pushes, I remembers, D brakes. Which one brakes oscillation?
objectives: Explain the P, I, and D roles in loop anatomy
Choose a tuning move from oscillation symptoms
evidence: Diagnoses underdamping and prescribes derivative action before proportional changes

scenarios.title: Anatomy of Organizational Feedback
scenarios.situation: A software company runs quarterly performance reviews, but product quality keeps sliding. Engineers say reviews measure lines of code and ticket counts; customer-escape defects are tracked by a different team and never enter the review. Managers say they are giving plenty of feedback.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the organizational feedback loop anatomically broken?
choices: The comparator: reviews compare engineers against the wrong reference (output volume instead of outcome quality), so correction pushes the wrong behavior
The effector: managers are not delivering the reviews forcefully enough
The setpoint: quarterly is too infrequent; reviews should be monthly
The sensor: engineers are not listening during review meetings
scenarios.why: The loop's comparator judges performance against its reference signal; here the reference is volume metrics while the true goal is quality, so the 'correction' actively rewards the wrong behavior. Frequency and delivery style cannot fix a comparator aimed at the wrong target.
scenarios.hint: Feedback is only as good as the reference it compares against. What is being compared to what?
objectives: Map sensor-comparator-effector anatomy onto a management process
Diagnose a mis-aimed comparator
evidence: Locates the fault at the comparator/reference and names the mis-aimed metric

scenarios.title: Anatomy of an Ecosystem Loop
scenarios.situation: A lake's algae blooms have worsened for five years. Data: fertilizer runoff (input) rose steadily; zooplankton that eat algae declined after a pesticide entered the water; dead algae decay consumes oxygen, killing fish that eat zooplankton. The town council proposes banning fertilizer outright as the single fix.
scenarios.prompt: Reading the lake as coupled feedback loops, how should you advise the council?
choices: Support the fertilizer ban alone: cutting the input starves the bloom, and single causes need single fixes

Advise a loop-level view: the bloom is driven by a reinforcing cycle (algae -> decay -> oxygen loss -> fewer grazers -> more algae) plus weakened negative feedback (pesticide killing zooplankton); intervene at multiple loop points, not just the input
Stock more fish: predators always restore balance in food webs
Do nothing: ecosystems self-correct and the bloom will collapse on its own
scenarios.why: The lake is coupled loops, not a single input-output pipe: a reinforcing loop amplifies the bloom while the pesticide has cut the negative-feedback grazing arm. Effective intervention must weaken the reinforcing cycle and restore the negative feedback together; an input ban alone leaves the loop structure intact.
scenarios.hint: Find the reinforcing loop and the damaged negative-feedback arm before prescribing.
objectives: Identify coupled reinforcing and balancing loops in an ecosystem
Argue for multi-point intervention from loop structure
evidence: Names the reinforcing cycle and the weakened grazing feedback, prescribing multi-point action

scenarios.title: Conversation as a Feedback System
scenarios.situation: Two co-founders argue weekly about product direction. Founder A states a position; Founder B hears criticism and defends; A hears defensiveness as closed-mindedness and pushes harder; B withdraws further. Each leaves believing the other will not listen. A coach suggests they prepare better arguments.
scenarios.prompt: Applying Bateson's view of communication as a feedback system, what is the actual pathology and the leverage point?
choices: Weak arguments: whoever argues better will break the cycle, so invest in rhetoric training
A symmetrical schismogenesis: each response amplifies the other's stance in a runaway positive-feedback loop; the leverage point is changing the pattern of response, not the content of arguments
A personality mismatch: the partnership is structurally unworkable and should be dissolved
Missing information: they need a shared dashboard so facts replace opinions
scenarios.why: Bateson named this symmetrical schismogenesis — a runaway positive-feedback loop where each party's move escalates the other's. Better arguments feed the loop (more push, more withdrawal). The intervention must target the response pattern itself: e.g., structured turn-taking that breaks the amplification circuit.
scenarios.hint: When each move makes the next move worse, the pattern — not the people or the points — is the problem.
objectives: Recognize symmetrical schismogenesis as positive feedback
Choose a pattern-level intervention over a content-level one
evidence: Names schismogenesis and prescribes changing the response pattern

scenarios.title: Anatomy of the Watt Governor
scenarios.situation: You are restoring an 1880s steam engine with its original centrifugal (Watt) governor: two flyballs spin with the engine, rise with speed, and close the steam valve as they rise. During testing the engine hunts — speed surges and sags rhythmically. The restoration team debates adding a modern electronic controller.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnosing the governor as a feedback loop, what explains the hunting and what is the minimal faithful fix?
choices: The flyballs are too light for this engine; replace them with heavier modern equivalents

Hunting is loop oscillation: the correction lags or overshoots (friction, play in the linkage, or excessive valve gain); the faithful fix is to reduce the loop gain or add damping in the linkage, preserving the original mechanism
The setpoint is wrong: adjust the spring tension until the hunting stops, ignoring the linkage
Install the electronic controller: 19th-century governors cannot hold speed on restored engines
scenarios.why: Hunting is the classic symptom of an underdamped feedback loop — delay or excess gain makes correction overshoot the setpoint rhythmically. The Watt governor already contains the full loop anatomy (sensor: flyballs, comparator: linkage geometry, effector: steam valve); the minimal fix tunes gain/damping in the existing loop rather than replacing its architecture.
scenarios.hint: Hunting means the loop overshoots. Do you need a new loop, or a calmer one?
objectives: Analyze a historical mechanism as a complete feedback loop
Distinguish tuning fixes from architectural replacement
evidence: Diagnoses hunting as underdamped oscillation and prescribes gain/damping adjustment

scenarios.title: Designing a Macy-Style Team
scenarios.situation: Your company is forming a task force on algorithmic hiring bias. The proposed roster is six machine-learning engineers. HR suggests adding a labor sociologist, an employment lawyer, and a former job applicant who experienced the system. Engineering leadership objects: outsiders will slow the technical work.
scenarios.prompt: What lesson from the Macy Conferences (1946-1953) settles this roster debate?
choices: The Macy lesson is specialization: keep the team purely technical so feedback concepts stay rigorous

The Macy breakthrough came from enforced interdisciplinarity — engineers, anthropologists, psychologists, and mathematicians in one room, sharing the language of feedback and information; the mixed roster is the method, not a concession
The Macy lesson is hierarchy: put the engineers in charge and consult outsiders only at the end
The Macy conferences failed precisely because of disciplinary mixing, so keep the team narrow
scenarios.why: The Macy Conferences deliberately assembled radically different disciplines around the shared concepts of circular causality, feedback, and information — and that collision produced cybernetics itself. A hiring-bias task force needs the same structure: the sociologist, lawyer, and affected applicant are not overhead, they are the feedback channels the engineers lack.
scenarios.hint: Cybernetics was born when disciplines collided in one room. What does that imply for the roster?
objectives: Explain the Macy Conferences' interdisciplinary method
Apply it to a modern team-design decision
evidence: Cites enforced interdisciplinarity as the Macy method and defends the mixed roster

scenarios.title: Circular Causality in a Family Business
scenarios.situation: In a family-run distributor, the founder micromanages his daughter, the operations lead. She responds by withholding bad news; he responds to surprises by tightening control; she withholds more. A consultant's report blames her communication skills and recommends training for her alone.
scenarios.prompt: The Macy circle would reject linear blame here. What is the cybernetically sound reframing?
choices: Accept the consultant's finding: the daughter's withholding is the root cause, and training fixes root causes

Reframe as circular causality: control provokes withholding which provokes control — each behavior is both cause and effect; intervene in the circuit (e.g., structured reporting rituals) rather than fixing one person
Blame the founder instead: reverse the linear blame to the true root cause
Remove family members from reporting lines: the only fix is structural separation
scenarios.why: The Macy core insight is circular causality: in a feedback circuit there is no first cause, only a pattern that sustains itself. Training one node leaves the circuit intact; the intervention must change the circuit — e.g., a weekly reporting ritual that makes withholding unnecessary and control redundant.
scenarios.hint: In a loop, who started it is the wrong question. What sustains it is the right one.
objectives: Apply circular causality to an interpersonal conflict
Reject linear blame in favor of circuit intervention
evidence: Describes the control-withholding circuit and proposes a circuit-level intervention

scenarios.title: Wiener vs von Bertalanffy on the Startup
scenarios.situation: Two advisors assess a struggling logistics startup. Advisor W says: map every feedback loop — dispatch, driver incentives, customer complaints — and tune the control mechanisms. Advisor B says: treat the firm as an open system exchanging matter, energy, and information with its environment; study its boundaries, inputs, and growth dynamics before touching any loop.
scenarios.prompt: Which advisor channels Wiener and which channels von Bertalanffy, and what is the productive synthesis?
choices: W is von Bertalanffy (feedback) and B is Wiener (open systems); pick W because feedback is the whole of systems science

W is Wiener (feedback, control, communication mechanisms) and B is von Bertalanffy (open systems, boundaries, wholeness); the synthesis is to bound the open system first, then tune its internal feedback loops
Both are Wiener: von Bertalanffy never wrote about organizations
Both are von Bertalanffy: Wiener's cybernetics applies only to machines, not firms
scenarios.why: Wiener's cybernetics centers control and communication through feedback; von Bertalanffy's General Systems Theory centers open systems, boundaries, and wholeness. They are complements: Bertalanffy tells you what the system is open to and where its boundaries lie; Wiener tells you how its internal loops regulate it. Diagnose the open system first, then tune the loops.
scenarios.hint: Wiener = feedback and control; Bertalanffy = open systems and wholeness. They answer different questions.
objectives: Contrast Wiener's cybernetics with von Bertalanffy's GST
Synthesize both framings on one case
evidence: Correctly attributes each advisor and orders the diagnosis: boundaries first, loops second

scenarios.title: Equifinality in Market Entry
scenarios.situation: Two rival food-delivery firms reach the same dominant city share by opposite routes: one burned venture capital on rider subsidies, the other built slowly through restaurant partnerships. Your strategy team insists there must be one best-practice playbook and wants to copy the subsidy route because it was faster.
scenarios.prompt: Von Bertalanffy's principle of equifinality speaks directly to this debate. What does it say?
choices: Equifinality proves the faster route is the optimal one; copy the subsidies

Equifinality states that open systems can reach the same final state from different initial conditions and by different paths; there is no single mandatory playbook — the team should match the path to its own resources and environment
Equifinality applies only to biological organisms, not companies
Equifinality means all strategies converge on failure; exit the market
scenarios.why: Equifinality — a signature von Bertalanffy concept for open systems — holds that the same end state can be reached via different trajectories. Copying the subsidy playbook ignores that the rival's path depended on its capital; the team's own resource base may favor the partnership path to the same outcome.
scenarios.hint: Same destination, different roads. What does that imply about 'best practice'?
objectives: Define equifinality
Use it to challenge playbook-copying in strategy
evidence: States equifinality and argues for path-resource fit over copying

scenarios.title: Bateson's Difference That Makes a Difference
scenarios.situation: An operations dashboard shows 40 real-time metrics, all green, yet the warehouse keeps missing ship targets. Managers stare at the wall of numbers daily and change nothing. The analytics vendor proposes adding 20 more metrics and an AI summary layer.
scenarios.prompt: Bateson defined information as 'a difference that makes a difference.' What does that prescribe for the dashboard?
choices: Add the 20 metrics: more differences measured means more information by definition
Cut the dashboard to the few differences that actually change decisions — a metric is information only if it makes a difference to action; the rest is noise regardless of volume
Keep all 40 but color-code them: presentation, not selection, is the problem
Replace the dashboard with the AI summary: automation resolves the overload
scenarios.why: Bateson's definition is pragmatic: a difference counts as information only insofar as it makes a difference — to the system that receives it. Forty green metrics that change no decision carry no information; the fix is subtractive, selecting the differences that trigger action, not additive.
scenarios.hint: If no decision changes, was any information transmitted?
objectives: Apply Bateson's definition of information
Prescribe subtractive dashboard design
evidence: Quotes the difference criterion and recommends cutting non-actionable metrics

scenarios.title: The Double Bind Memo
scenarios.situation: A CEO sends an all-hands memo: 'I want radical candor — challenge every decision openly. But remember, we are a family, and family members do not embarrass each other in public.' Afterwards, engineers who raise concerns in meetings are praised for candor and quietly passed over for promotion. Silence spreads.
scenarios.prompt: Bateson's double-bind theory diagnoses this precisely. What is the bind, and what breaks it?
choices: There is no bind: employees should simply be more courageous about candor

The bind is two contradictory injunctions at different levels (speak up / do not embarrass) with punishment for either response and no permitted meta-commentary; it breaks by making the contradiction discussable — legitimizing talk about the talk
The bind is a compensation problem: pay people more to tolerate the contradiction
The bind resolves by choosing one injunction: enforce candor and abolish the family metaphor by decree
scenarios.why: Bateson's double bind requires: two conflicting injunctions, punishment whichever is obeyed, and no escape to a meta-level where the contradiction can be named. The memo creates exactly this. Decreeing one side wins does not restore the missing meta-level; only legitimizing discussion of the contradiction itself dissolves the bind.
scenarios.hint: Two orders, punished either way, and you are forbidden to mention the contradiction. What is missing?
objectives: Identify a double bind in organizational communication
Prescribe the meta-level escape
evidence: Names the two injunctions and prescribes legitimizing meta-communication

scenarios.title: McCulloch-Pitts in the Neural Net Era
scenarios.situation: A junior ML engineer dismisses the 1943 McCulloch-Pitts neuron as a historical curiosity: 'Binary threshold units have nothing to do with our transformer models.' Her tech lead disagrees but struggles to articulate the connection in one breath.
scenarios.prompt: What is the precise, defensible relevance of McCulloch and Pitts (1943) to modern deep learning?
choices: None: transformers abandoned threshold logic entirely, so the paper is only of antiquarian interest

The paper proved networks of simple threshold units can compute any logical function — establishing the principle that cognition-like computation can emerge from interconnected simple units, the architectural idea every neural network, including transformers, still instantiates
The paper invented backpropagation, which transformers still use unchanged
The paper proved binary units are optimal, so modern continuous activations are a mistake
scenarios.why: 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity' showed that networks of idealized binary threshold neurons can realize arbitrary logical functions — the founding demonstration that mind-like computation could arise from simple interconnected units. Transformers differ in scale, training, and continuous activations, but they inherit this exact architectural premise.
scenarios.hint: What did the paper prove possible — not how modern nets train, but what networks of simple units can compute?
objectives: State the McCulloch-Pitts result accurately
Connect it to modern neural architectures without overclaiming
evidence: States the logical-completeness result and its architectural legacy

scenarios.title: Wiener's Refusal
scenarios.situation: Your robotics lab is offered a lucrative defense contract to adapt its warehouse navigation stack for autonomous weapons targeting. The funding would triple the lab's budget. A senior researcher cites Norbert Wiener and argues the lab should decline, even though the work is 'just navigation math.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the Wiener precedent, and how does it apply to the 'just math' defense?
choices: Wiener had no ethical positions; he accepted all military funding, so there is no precedent

Wiener, whose wartime anti-aircraft predictor work founded cybernetics, later refused military research funding and warned in 'The Human Use of Human Beings' about ceding human judgment to machines — the precedent is that the mathematician is responsible for foreseeable uses, and 'just math' does not absolve the lab
Wiener's precedent is that scientists should never consider applications at all
Wiener supported autonomous weapons, so the precedent favors accepting
scenarios.why: Wiener's trajectory is the point: the founder of cybernetics did the wartime predictor work, then publicly refused further military funding and spent 'The Human Use of Human Beings' warning against dehumanizing automation. The precedent holds that technical neutrality is no defense — responsibility follows foreseeable use.
scenarios.hint: The man who built the wartime predictor later refused the war work. What does that say about 'just math'?
objectives: Recall Wiener's ethical stance accurately
Apply it to a dual-use funding decision
evidence: Cites the predictor work, the refusal, and the responsibility principle

domains.name: Feedback, Control & Homeostasis
domains.description: The technical core: negative/positive feedback, control theory basics, and stability.

scenarios.title: The Thermostat That Hunts
scenarios.situation: A building's HVAC oscillates: freezing blasts alternate with stuffy warmth every 20 minutes. The thermostat is new. The facilities team blames the boiler.
scenarios.prompt: Apply feedback analysis. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The boiler is oversized — replace it with a smaller unit

Excessive gain and/or sensor-actuator delay: the thermostat overcorrects (full blast) and the temperature sensor is far from the vents, so correction arrives late — classic delayed negative feedback oscillation. Fix: reduce differential/gain, relocate sensor, or add anticipation
The thermostat is defective — replace it
Occupants keep changing the setpoint
scenarios.why: Oscillation in a negative-feedback loop signals gain/delay mismatch, not component failure: the system corrects too hard, too late, overshoots, then corrects back. The 20-minute period IS the diagnostic — it reflects the loop's delay. The fix is control-theoretic (lower gain, faster sensing, anticipation), not mechanical replacement. Blaming the boiler is component thinking; the answer is loop thinking.
scenarios.hint: The system oscillates with a regular period. What in a feedback loop creates oscillation?
objectives: Feedback analysis
Gain and delay
Oscillation
evidence: BMS trend
Supply temp oscillates ±6°C with 20-min period; setpoint constant.
Layout
Thermostat 15m from nearest vent, behind a partition.

scenarios.title: Finding Loops in the Support Org
scenarios.situation: A SaaS company's support queue grows every quarter despite hiring. You map the system: tickets arrive from customers; agents close tickets; management rewards agents per ticket closed; agents, pressed for speed, close tickets with shallow fixes; shallow fixes generate reopened tickets and new complaints; management sees rising volume and hires more agents, who are onboarded with the same speed incentives.
scenarios.prompt: Which intervention actually changes the loop structure rather than feeding it?
choices: Hire faster: more agents with the same incentives will eventually drain the queue
Change the reward to reward durable resolution (low reopen rate), breaking the shallow-fix reinforcing loop at its incentive link
Add a triage layer: more process steps will absorb the volume
Outsource tier-1 support to cut cost per ticket
scenarios.why: The mapped system is a reinforcing loop: speed incentives -> shallow fixes -> reopens -> more volume -> more speed pressure. Hiring and triage add capacity without touching the loop's gain; only changing what is rewarded alters the loop structure itself, converting a vicious cycle into a balancing one.
scenarios.hint: Draw the loop. Which arrow can you actually rewire?
objectives: Map reinforcing loops in an organization
Choose a structural intervention over a capacity one
evidence: Names the speed->shallow-fix->reopen loop and rewires the incentive link

scenarios.title: Designing Negative Feedback for Cloud Spend
scenarios.situation: Your startup's cloud bill tripled in six months. Engineers spin up resources freely; finance sees the bill 30 days later; by the time anyone reacts, the spend is entrenched. The CFO proposes a monthly approval committee for all new resources.
scenarios.prompt: Design the cybernetically sound negative-feedback control. What matters most?
choices: The monthly committee: human approval is the strongest possible negative feedback

Shorten the feedback delay and close the loop at the source: real-time spend dashboards per team with automatic alerts and budget guardrails at provisioning time, so deviation corrects before it compounds
Negotiate a bigger enterprise discount: lower unit cost solves the growth
Blame engineering culture: the problem is attitudes, not loops
scenarios.why: Negative feedback stabilizes only if the correction arrives while it can still act — a 30-day delay plus a monthly committee lets overshoot compound between corrections. Effective control shortens the loop (real-time visibility) and places the comparator at the decision point (provisioning guardrails), which is the actual negative-feedback design.
scenarios.hint: A thermostat that reads the temperature a month late cannot hold the setpoint. Where is the delay?
objectives: Design a negative-feedback control for a cost system
Explain why feedback delay defeats correction
evidence: Proposes real-time visibility plus provisioning-time guardrails, citing delay

scenarios.title: Spotting the Runaway: A Bank Run in Miniature
scenarios.situation: A regional bank faces rumors of insolvency on social media. A few depositors withdraw; local news films the ATM lines; more depositors see the lines and withdraw; the bank, seeing outflows, restricts withdrawals, which confirms the rumor. The bank is actually solvent, with reserves well above requirements.
scenarios.prompt: Name the loop dynamics and the correct early intervention.
choices: A balancing loop that will self-correct once the rumor fades; do nothing and wait

A runaway positive-feedback loop (withdrawals -> visible lines -> more withdrawals, amplified by restrictions); the intervention is to break the amplification early — credible, verifiable disclosure of reserves plus visible normal operations before the loop saturates
A negative-feedback loop: restrictions will stabilize outflows, so tighten them faster
A linear cause-effect chain: find and punish the rumor's originator to stop it
scenarios.why: Each withdrawal visibly signals danger, recruiting the next withdrawal — positive feedback with no natural ceiling until the bank empties. Withdrawal restrictions act as confirming evidence, adding gain. Only an early counter-signal stronger than the loop's amplification (transparent, verifiable solvency proof while operations look normal) can break it before saturation.
scenarios.hint: Does each event make the next event more or less likely? That tells you the loop sign.
objectives: Identify runaway positive feedback in a social system
Prescribe an early amplification-breaking intervention
evidence: Names the positive-feedback loop and prescribes early credible disclosure

scenarios.title: The Hiring Oscillation
scenarios.situation: A logistics firm alternates between frantic hiring binges and layoffs every 18 months. The pattern: a capacity crunch triggers aggressive hiring; recruiting and training take 9 months; by the time new staff are productive, demand has normalized, so the firm is overstaffed; layoffs follow; months later another crunch hits. Management blames 'unpredictable markets.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the cybernetic diagnosis, and what breaks the cycle?
choices: The market is genuinely unpredictable; the cycle is unavoidable and should be managed with severance planning

Delay-induced oscillation: the 9-month hiring delay means corrections arrive out of phase with the need, so the firm perpetually overshoots; the fix is to shorten the delay (faster onboarding, flexible staffing buffers) or damp the correction (hire to a moving average, not the peak)
Managers are incompetent at forecasting; replace them with a forecasting algorithm
The hiring gain is too low; hire even more aggressively during crunches
scenarios.why: This is the classic delay-oscillation pattern Donella Meadows described: when corrective action lags the signal by a large fraction of the cycle, each correction lands out of phase and overshoots, producing perpetual boom-bust. The cure targets the delay and the gain — faster response, buffered capacity, and hiring to smoothed demand — not better predictions of an 'unpredictable' market.
scenarios.hint: Nine months of delay in an 18-month cycle: corrections keep arriving exactly out of phase.
objectives: Diagnose delay-induced oscillation
Prescribe delay-shortening and gain-damping fixes
evidence: Names delay-induced oscillation and proposes buffering plus smoothed hiring targets

scenarios.title: The PID Tuning Decision
scenarios.situation: You are tuning the temperature controller for a chemical reactor. Trial A (high proportional gain): reaches setpoint in 4 minutes but overshoots by 15 degrees, risking a runaway reaction. Trial B (low gain): no overshoot but takes 40 minutes, and a persistent 3-degree offset remains because the integral term is disabled. The batch is worth $200,000 and the safety margin is 10 degrees.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tuning judgment?
choices: Ship Trial A: speed matters most and 15 degrees of overshoot is acceptable risk
Ship Trial B: safety first, and the 3-degree offset is a minor quality issue

Reject both: enable the integral term to eliminate the offset in Trial B's safe structure, then add derivative damping and re-test — tune for no overshoot beyond the 10-degree safety margin with zero steady-state error
Average the two gains: the midpoint of two bad tunings is a good tuning
scenarios.why: Trial A violates the hard safety constraint (15-degree overshoot > 10-degree margin) — unacceptable regardless of speed. Trial B is safe but leaves steady-state error because the integrator is off. The disciplined move is structural: keep the safe low-gain base, enable integral action to kill the offset, add derivative damping against overshoot, and verify against the safety margin. Tuning is constraint-first, not compromise-by-averaging.
scenarios.hint: Safety margin is a hard constraint, and the missing integrator has a name for its symptom: steady-state error.
objectives: Apply safety-constrained PID tuning judgment
Explain integral action's role in eliminating offset
evidence: Rejects the unsafe trial, prescribes I-enable plus D-damping within the safety margin

scenarios.title: Feedforward vs Feedback on the Highway Crew
scenarios.situation: A highway maintenance crew is repeatedly caught by flash floods that wash out fresh asphalt. They currently react after each flood (feedback): assess damage, repave, wait for the next storm. A meteorologist offers a paid early-warning feed; the crew chief says warnings are useless because 'you can't control the weather.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the cybernetic case for the early-warning feed?
choices: There is none: feedback after the event is the only honest control, since the weather is uncontrollable

Feedforward control: the warning measures the disturbance before it hits, allowing pre-emptive action (cover fresh asphalt, reschedule pours) — it complements feedback by acting on measured disturbance rather than waiting for error
Replace feedback entirely: with warnings, post-storm assessment becomes unnecessary
The feed is only useful if it is perfectly accurate; imperfect forecasts add noise
scenarios.why: Feedforward measures the disturbance directly and acts before error appears, while feedback corrects after error appears; they are complements, not rivals. The chief's objection confuses controlling the weather (impossible) with controlling the response to it (the whole point). Even imperfect forecasts beat pure reaction when the cost of being caught unprepared is high.
scenarios.hint: Feedback corrects error after it appears. What acts before the error appears?
objectives: Distinguish feedforward from feedback control
Justify feedforward under uncertainty
evidence: Defines feedforward as disturbance-measurement and pairs it with existing feedback

scenarios.title: Nested Loops in the Sales Organization
scenarios.situation: A sales org has two loops: reps adjust daily effort against weekly targets (fast inner loop), and leadership adjusts quarterly quotas and territories against revenue goals (slow outer loop). Lately the outer loop raises quotas every quarter based on last quarter's over-performance, and reps respond by sandbagging deals into the next quarter — total revenue is flat while everyone games the system.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnose the nested-loop pathology and fix it.
choices: Tighten the inner loop: daily monitoring of rep activity will stop sandbagging

The outer loop is destabilizing the inner: quota ratcheting punishes over-performance, so the inner loop's rational response is to hide performance; fix the outer loop's reference (e.g., quotas set from market potential, with ratchet caps) so the inner loop can optimize honestly
Abolish quotas: without targets there is nothing to game
Speed up the outer loop to monthly quota resets so sandbagging has nowhere to hide
scenarios.why: In nested loops the outer loop sets the reference the inner loop chases; when the outer loop punishes success (ratcheting quotas up after over-performance), the inner loop rationally suppresses its own output — the pathology is in the outer reference, not inner effort. Faster or tighter inner control just intensifies the gaming. The fix re-anchors the outer reference to market potential with anti-ratchet rules.
scenarios.hint: The inner loop is behaving rationally given its reference. Who sets that reference?
objectives: Analyze nested feedback loops
Locate pathology in the outer loop's reference signal
evidence: Identifies quota ratcheting as the outer-loop fault and re-anchors quotas to market potential

domains.name: Information, Entropy & Communication
domains.description: Shannon meets Wiener: measuring information, channel capacity, and the entropy connection.

scenarios.title: The Noisy Channel
scenarios.situation: A Mars rover link has 1 kHz bandwidth and the signal is barely above noise (SNR ≈ 1, i.e., 0 dB). The team debates buying a bigger antenna (more bandwidth) vs a better amplifier (better SNR).
scenarios.prompt: Use Shannon-Hartley to advise. C = B log2(1 + S/N).
choices: Buy bandwidth: double B to 2 kHz — capacity doubles to ~2 kbps

Compute first: current C = 1000 × log2(2) = 1 kbps. Doubling B → 2 kbps. But improving SNR from 1 to 3 (same cost as the antenna?) → C = 1000 × log2(4) = 2 kbps too. The log means SNR improvements have diminishing returns — get actual quotes, then decide; also consider coding (error correction) which the formula assumes is optimal
SNR does not matter — only bandwidth counts
The formula is theoretical — ignore it and test both
scenarios.why: Shannon-Hartley makes the trade-off quantitative: at SNR=1, capacity scales linearly with B but only logarithmically with S/N — so the FIRST SNR doubling (1→3) matches a bandwidth doubling, but the next doubling buys less. The engineering answer needs costs: $/kHz vs $/dB, plus coding gains (modern codes approach capacity). The formula does not pick the winner — it prices the options so the budget can.
scenarios.hint: Plug both options into C = B log2(1+S/N). Which buys more bits per dollar?
objectives: Shannon-Hartley
Channel capacity
Trade-off analysis
evidence: Link
B = 1 kHz, SNR ≈ 1 (0 dB) → C ≈ 1 kbps.
Quotes
Antenna (2x B): $X. Amplifier (SNR 1→3): $Y.

scenarios.title: Entropy of a Biased Coin
scenarios.situation: A sensor reports a binary status each second. Under normal conditions the reading is 0 with probability 0.75 and 1 with probability 0.25. A vendor proposes compressing the telemetry stream and claims 'each reading carries 1 bit of information, so the stream is incompressible.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual Shannon entropy per reading, and what does it imply?
choices: 1 bit, as the vendor says: binary readings always carry exactly 1 bit
Approximately 0.81 bits: H = -(0.75*log2(0.75) + 0.25*log2(0.25)) ~ 0.81, so the stream is compressible to about 81% of its raw size with ideal coding
0.5 bits: the minority symbol carries half a bit
2 bits: uncertainty doubles because the distribution is skewed
scenarios.why: Shannon entropy for this distribution is -(0.75 x log2 0.75 + 0.25 x log2 0.25) = 0.311 + 0.5 = 0.811 bits per symbol — less than 1 because the skewed distribution is partly predictable. The source coding theorem says the stream can be compressed to near 0.81 bits per reading; the vendor's '1 bit always' claim is false.
scenarios.hint: Skewed means predictable, and predictable means less surprise per symbol. Compute -sum(p log2 p).
objectives: Compute Shannon entropy for a binary source
Apply the source coding theorem to a compression claim
evidence: Computes ~0.81 bits and concludes the stream is compressible

scenarios.title: Channel Capacity on a Noisy Link
scenarios.situation: A remote pipeline monitor must send 50 kbps of sensor data over a radio link with 3 kHz of bandwidth. The link budget gives a signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB (a power ratio of 1000:1). The radio vendor guarantees 'up to 100 kbps' on this channel.
scenarios.prompt: Does the Shannon-Hartley law support the vendor's guarantee for your 50 kbps need?
choices: Yes: 100 kbps guaranteed exceeds the 50 kbps need, so deploy with confidence

No: capacity C = 3000 x log2(1+1000) ~ 29.9 kbps, which is below both the guarantee and your 50 kbps need — the vendor's claim violates the Shannon limit, so you need more bandwidth, better SNR, or less data
Yes, because 30 dB is a strong signal and strong signals carry unlimited data
No, but the fix is a better antenna rather than questioning the guarantee
scenarios.why: Shannon-Hartley caps capacity at B x log2(1+S/N) = 3000 x log2(1001) ~= 29.9 kbps — a hard physical ceiling no coding can exceed. The vendor's 100 kbps guarantee is impossible on this channel, and the 50 kbps requirement cannot be met without more bandwidth, higher SNR, or data reduction.
scenarios.hint: C = B log2(1 + S/N). Run the numbers before trusting the datasheet.
objectives: Apply the Shannon-Hartley capacity formula
Use it to falsify an impossible vendor claim
evidence: Computes ~30 kbps capacity and rejects the 100 kbps guarantee

scenarios.title: The Redundancy Decision
scenarios.situation: A spacecraft team debates its command uplink coding. Option R: heavy redundancy (triple repetition) — extremely reliable but only 1/3 the command rate. Option E: efficient coding near the Shannon limit — full rate but any uncorrected error corrupts a command. The mission phase involves rare, critical, irreversible commands (engine burns).
scenarios.prompt: How should information theory guide the coding choice for this phase?
choices: Always choose efficiency: Shannon proved we can approach capacity with arbitrarily low error, so redundancy is wasteful

Match redundancy to the cost of error: for rare, critical, irreversible commands, the price of a corrupted burn dwarfs the bandwidth cost, so spend redundancy heavily here and use efficient coding for routine telemetry
Always choose triple repetition: reliability is the only metric that matters in space
Let the ground operators decide per command with no policy: flexibility beats theory
scenarios.why: Information theory frames the trade precisely: redundancy buys error protection at the price of rate. Shannon's limit tells us what is achievable, but the choice of operating point is economic — set by the asymmetry between bandwidth cost and error cost. Irreversible critical commands justify heavy redundancy; bulk routine data justifies efficiency.
scenarios.hint: Redundancy is insurance. When is the insured event catastrophic?
objectives: Explain the redundancy-rate trade-off
Set the operating point from error cost
evidence: Justifies heavy redundancy for critical commands from error-cost asymmetry

scenarios.title: Signal vs Noise in the Incident Channel
scenarios.situation: A DevOps team's alert channel fires 400 alerts a day; 3 are actionable. Engineers muted the channel months ago. Last week a genuine database-failover alert scrolled past unnoticed and caused a 2-hour outage. The proposed fix is 'smarter alert routing with machine learning.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the information-theoretic diagnosis, and the first fix?
choices: A routing problem: ML triage will surface the 3 real alerts without changing alert volume

A signal-to-noise collapse: with 397 noise alerts per 3 signals, the channel's effective capacity for attention is saturated — the first fix is subtractive (kill noisy alerts, alert only on actionable, paged-worthy conditions), because no receiver can extract signal from that noise ratio
An engineer discipline problem: unmute the channel and mandate attention
A tooling problem: buy a louder paging system
scenarios.why: Attention is a channel with finite capacity; a 397:3 noise-to-signal ratio means the receiver (the engineer) cannot extract the signal no matter how it is routed — this is Shannon's lesson applied to human attention. The fix must raise the SNR at the source by deleting non-actionable alerts, not by adding smarter plumbing downstream of the noise.
scenarios.hint: If 99% of a channel is noise, is the problem the receiver or the transmitter?
objectives: Apply signal-to-noise reasoning to alerting
Prescribe subtractive alert hygiene
evidence: Diagnoses SNR collapse and prescribes deleting non-actionable alerts first

scenarios.title: Requisite Variety in the Board Pack
scenarios.situation: A manufacturing board receives a 200-page monthly pack, yet every strategic surprise of the last two years (a supplier failure, a demand collapse, a quality scandal) arrived with no prior signal in the pack. The CFO's solution is a 300-page pack with more detail.
scenarios.prompt: Combine Ashby and Shannon: why does more pages not mean more control, and what would?
choices: It does mean more control: 300 pages carry more bits, and more bits always improve regulation

Bits are not the binding constraint — relevant variety is: the pack must carry variety that matches the disturbances that actually threaten the firm (supplier, demand, quality signals), with the noise of routine detail stripped out; a 20-page pack of decision-relevant differences beats a 300-page undifferentiated dump
The board needs fewer meetings, not better packs
Surprises are unforeseeable by definition; no pack design helps
scenarios.why: Ashby's law demands the regulator's variety match the disturbance variety that matters — supplier, demand, and quality channels were absent, so no page count could compensate. Shannon adds that a channel stuffed with routine detail has low effective signal. Control improves by selecting the differences that make a difference (Bateson) and giving them a short, fast path to the board.
scenarios.hint: The surprises had no signal in the pack. What variety was missing — and what variety was noise?
objectives: Combine requisite variety with signal-to-noise reasoning
Redesign reporting for decision-relevant variety
evidence: Identifies missing disturbance variety and prescribes a short decision-relevant pack

scenarios.title: Shannon vs Meaning in the Contract Clause
scenarios.situation: A legal-tech startup advertises 'Shannon-optimal compression of contracts — maximum information density.' A pilot customer compresses a 50-page supply agreement to a dense 5-page symbol stream that no lawyer can read, then discovers a liability clause was 'losslessly preserved but semantically invisible' to every reviewer.
scenarios.prompt: What is the precise conceptual error in the startup's claim?
choices: The compression was lossy: true Shannon-optimal coding would have preserved readability

Category error: Shannon information measures surprise/uncertainty reduction, explicitly excluding meaning — 'maximum information density' in Shannon's sense says nothing about semantic accessibility, which is what contracts require; the startup sold a syntactic metric as a semantic guarantee
The customer needed a bigger screen, not a conceptual correction
Shannon's theory does not apply to text at all
scenarios.why: Shannon famously bracketed semantics: his theory quantifies uncertainty reduction, deliberately saying nothing about meaning. A 'Shannon-optimal' encoding can be perfectly information-preserving yet semantically opaque. The startup's error is selling a syntactic optimum as if it guaranteed the pragmatic property — human interpretability — that contracts actually need.
scenarios.hint: Shannon himself said semantics were irrelevant to the engineering problem. What problem is a contract?
objectives: State the scope limit of Shannon information (excludes semantics)
Diagnose a category error in a product claim
evidence: Names the syntax/semantics category error in the startup's claim

scenarios.title: How Much Information Does Control Need?
scenarios.situation: A warehouse deploys robots regulated by a central controller. The controller receives each robot's full 4K video feed (25 Mbps per robot, 40 robots) but issues only simple commands: forward, stop, turn, lift. The network is saturated, commands lag 2 seconds, and robots collide. The vendor proposes upgrading to 8K cameras 'for better control.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the cybernetic view of information-for-control prescribe?
choices: Upgrade the cameras: better sensing always improves control, and bandwidth can be bought

The controller needs only the information its commands can act on: 4 discrete commands need a few bits of relevant state (position, obstacle proximity, load status), not gigabits of video — cut sensing to decision-relevant state, move perception to the edge, and the 2-second lag (a feedback delay) disappears with the bandwidth
Add more central servers: the problem is compute, not information
Slow the robots down: speed is the only adjustable parameter
scenarios.why: Control requires only the variety the regulator can actually use — Ashby again: a 4-command regulator needs bits of relevant state, not video streams. The 4K feeds are noise relative to the control task, and their bandwidth cost creates the real pathology: 2 seconds of feedback delay. Edge perception plus minimal state reporting fixes both the information mismatch and the delay.
scenarios.hint: Four possible commands. How many bits of state does each command actually need?
objectives: Apply 'information needed for control' reasoning
Diagnose feedback delay caused by sensing overload
evidence: Reduces sensing to command-relevant state and moves perception to the edge

domains.name: Second-Order Cybernetics
domains.description: The observer observed: reflexivity, autopoiesis, and von Foerster's ethical turn.

scenarios.title: The Metric That Ate the Team
scenarios.situation: After introducing 'tickets closed per day' as the team KPI, ticket counts soared — but customer satisfaction fell and engineers report splitting single issues into multiples.
scenarios.prompt: Analyze with second-order cybernetics.
choices: The engineers are unethical — discipline them

Observer effect / Goodhart's law: the measurement intervened in the system — agents optimized the metric, not the goal. The KPI (observer's distinction) reshaped the observed work. Fix: measure outcomes (satisfaction, resolution quality), involve the team in metric design, and treat metrics as fallible lenses
The KPI target was set too low — raise it
Tickets got easier — the metric is fine
scenarios.why: Second-order insight: the observer is inside the system. The metric did not neutrally record work — it reorganized it (splitting tickets, rushing closures). Goodhart's law is the folk version; von Foerster's point is deeper: every distinction the observer draws (what counts as 'a ticket') constructs the reality it claims to measure. The fix is reflexive: co-design metrics with the measured, track outcomes over outputs, and expect gaming as data about the metric — not about morals.
scenarios.hint: Who is inside the system here — just the engineers, or the metric designer too?
objectives: Second-order cybernetics
Goodhart's law
Reflexivity
evidence: Metrics
Tickets/day +40%; CSAT -18%; reopen rate +25%.
Interviews
'We split multi-part issues now — it counts more.'

scenarios.title: The Hawthorne Audit
scenarios.situation: A factory pilots a productivity-monitoring program in one hall: output rises 18% in six weeks. Management declares the monitoring system a success and rolls it out plant-wide. In the second hall, output rises only 4% and falls back within two months. An analyst notes the pilot hall knew it was being studied.
scenarios.prompt: What is the second-order cybernetic reading of the pilot result?
choices: The pilot proves monitoring works; the second hall needs stricter enforcement of the same system

The 18% likely includes an observer effect — being observed changed the observed (the Hawthorne pattern); the pilot measured the system-plus-observer, not the monitoring tool alone, so rollout on the tool's merits is unjustified without a controlled comparison
The pilot hall had better workers; the result is a sampling artifact with no observer component
Productivity cannot be measured at all, so abandon all monitoring
scenarios.why: Second-order cybernetics insists the observer is part of the system: measurement perturbs what it measures. The pilot hall's awareness of being studied is itself an intervention, so the 18% confounds tool effect with observer effect. A valid claim needs the observer's influence isolated — otherwise the rollout exports an illusion.
scenarios.hint: Who else was in the pilot hall besides the workers? The watchers.
objectives: Explain the observer effect in measurement
Withhold causal claims from confounded pilots
evidence: Names the observer effect and demands a controlled comparison before rollout

scenarios.title: Goodhart at the Call Center
scenarios.situation: A support center bonuses agents on low average handle time (AHT). Within a quarter, AHT falls 30% — and customer satisfaction collapses, reopen rates double, and agents report hanging up on complex callers. Leadership's response is to tighten the AHT target further.
scenarios.prompt: Apply Goodhart's Law. What happened, and what is the structurally sound response?
choices: Agents are gaming the metric: punish the worst offenders and the metric will recover its validity

When AHT became the target, it ceased to be a good measure — agents optimized the measure instead of the goal (resolved customers), a textbook Goodhart/Campbell effect; the fix is to re-anchor evaluation to outcomes (resolution quality, satisfaction) and treat metrics as fallible indicators, not targets
The metric is fine but the target was too lax; tightening further will restore discipline
Abolish all metrics: measurement inherently corrupts service work
scenarios.why: Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Agents rationally optimized what was rewarded, destroying the metric's validity as an indicator of good service. Punishing gamers or tightening the target intensifies the distortion; the structural fix changes what is targeted — outcomes, with metrics as servants, not masters.
scenarios.hint: The agents did exactly what was rewarded. Was the reward aimed at the right thing?
objectives: State Goodhart's Law
Redesign incentives from metric-targets to outcome-anchors
evidence: Names the Goodhart effect and re-anchors evaluation to resolution outcomes

scenarios.title: Teaching to the Test
scenarios.situation: A school district ties funding to standardized math scores. Scores rise steadily for four years. Meanwhile, independent assessments of problem-solving show no gain, teachers report dropping science projects to drill test formats, and arts periods vanish. The superintendent cites the scores as proof of improvement.
scenarios.prompt: A second-order cybernetician evaluating this 'improvement' would argue what?
choices: The scores prove real improvement: standardized tests are objective and drill is effective pedagogy

The measurement system has reconfigured the system it measures (Campbell's Law): the district optimized the indicator, not learning — scores now measure test-preparation, and the superintendent's claim confuses the map (scores) with the territory (education); validate against independent, un-incentivized measures
The problem is teacher quality: replace the staff and scores will reflect real learning
More subjects should be tied to funding to spread the incentive evenly
scenarios.why: This is Campbell's Law in the wild: high-stakes indicators get corrupted by the pressures applied to them. The system under observation reorganized itself around the observer's instrument — curriculum narrowed to what the test samples. Scores remain 'true' as measurements of test-taking while becoming false as measurements of learning; only un-incentivized instruments can check the claim.
scenarios.hint: The territory (learning) reshaped itself to flatter the map (scores). Which one is the superintendent reading?
objectives: Apply Campbell's Law to high-stakes testing
Distinguish indicator validity from goal achievement
evidence: Names Campbell's Law and demands validation by un-incentivized measures

scenarios.title: The Self-Reference Survey
scenarios.situation: A company runs an engagement survey asking employees to rate, on a 1-5 scale, 'how much you trust this survey to remain anonymous.' The item scores 2.1. HR reports 'trust in the survey process is low' and commissions a follow-up survey on survey trust, with a cover letter promising anonymity.
scenarios.prompt: What is the self-referential trap here, and what breaks it?
choices: There is no trap: low trust is a straightforward finding, and more surveying will diagnose it

The instrument measures its own credibility — a self-referential loop where distrust of the medium contaminates every message it carries, including the distrust reading itself; the escape is not another survey but a change of medium (e.g., trusted third-party interviews, verifiable anonymity mechanisms) that sits outside the loop
The trap is the 1-5 scale: switch to open text and the paradox dissolves
HR should simply assert anonymity more forcefully in the next cover letter
scenarios.why: Second-order paradox: the survey asks the system to evaluate the survey, so the reading is entangled with the instrument's own standing — a 2.1 may measure distrust of this survey specifically, or honest reporting through it; the instrument cannot separate the two. Another survey repeats the entanglement. Only an observation channel outside the loop (independent interviewers, structural anonymity guarantees) breaks the self-reference.
scenarios.hint: Can a ruler measure its own accuracy? What observes the observer?
objectives: Identify self-referential measurement paradoxes
Prescribe an observation channel outside the loop
evidence: Names the self-referential entanglement and proposes an independent channel

scenarios.title: The Ethics of the Model
scenarios.situation: A city pilots an algorithm that allocates building-inspection priority from historical violation data. The model sends inspectors overwhelmingly to one neighborhood — the same neighborhood historically over-inspected, hence over-represented in the data. Officials call the model 'objective because it is mathematical.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the second-order ethical objection, stated precisely?
choices: There is none: mathematics cannot be biased, so the allocation is fair by definition

The model closes a self-fulfilling loop: past observation intensity shapes the data, the data shapes the model, the model directs future observation to the same places, confirming itself — the 'objectivity' claim hides that the observer's history is baked into the instrument; ethics requires auditing the loop, not just the math
The objection is only about accuracy: with more data the bias would vanish
The fix is to remove the neighborhood variable: blindness guarantees fairness
scenarios.why: Second-order cybernetics locates ethics in the observer-system relation: the model is not a neutral mirror but a participant that steers future observations to confirm its own past. 'Objective because mathematical' mistakes the map for the territory while hiding the loop. Removing one variable does not break the feedback; the ethical demand is to make the whole observation-allocation loop visible and contestable.
scenarios.hint: Where did the training data come from? Who decided to look there first?
objectives: Expose self-confirming observation loops in algorithmic systems
Argue the ethical locus is the loop, not the equation
evidence: Traces the data->model->inspection->data loop and demands loop-level auditing

scenarios.title: Participatory Design, Beer's Way
scenarios.situation: A hospital network is designing productivity metrics for nursing wards. The analytics team proposes deriving metrics from EHR timestamps alone. The nurses' union demands co-design of the metrics, citing Stafford Beer's work. The CFO worries co-design will let nurses 'choose easy metrics.'
scenarios.prompt: How does second-order cybernetics (and Beer's practice) adjudicate this?
choices: Side with the CFO: the observed must not design the observation, or metrics lose objectivity

Side with the nurses: in second-order cybernetics the distinction between observer and observed is a choice, and viable systems need the measured to participate in defining the measure — Beer's teams built metrics with workers because ownership of the model is what makes regulation work; the safeguard is transparent, jointly-owned definitions, not exclusion
Compromise: let analysts design the metrics and nurses vote yes/no at the end
Abandon metrics: nursing cannot be measured without distortion
scenarios.why: Von Foerster's second-order move dissolves the observer/observed split: those inside the system are observers too. Beer put this into practice — viable regulation requires the regulated to own the model, because a metric imposed from outside becomes a target to game (Goodhart), while a jointly-defined metric becomes a shared instrument. The CFO's fear is answered by transparency of definitions, not by excluding the observed.
scenarios.hint: Who has to live inside the metric? What happens when they had no hand in it?
objectives: Justify participatory metric design from second-order principles
Connect Beer's practice to Goodhart resistance
evidence: Argues for co-designed, jointly-owned metrics citing observer/observed unity

scenarios.title: The Therapist in the System
scenarios.situation: A family therapist notices that whenever she asks the parents about their conflict, the teenage son's disruptive behavior spikes in the session — and the parents unite around managing him, dropping their own conflict. Her supervisor suggests the son's pathology is simply 'more severe than assessed.'
scenarios.prompt: Apply Bateson's second-order insight to the therapy room itself.
choices: Accept the supervisor's view: escalate the son's individual treatment plan

Recognize the therapist as part of the circuit: her questions are inputs the family system processes — the son's escalation functions as negative feedback stabilizing the parents' conflict by redirecting it; the 'pathology' may be a property of the therapist-inclusive system, so she must vary her own interventions as experiments on the circuit she participates in
Exclude the son from sessions: remove the disruptive node to treat the parents cleanly
Record sessions for a second therapist to rate objectively from outside
scenarios.why: Bateson's cybernetic view of therapy treats the family-plus-therapist as one circuit: the son's symptom can be the system's homeostatic correction, triggered by the therapist's own input. There is no outside vantage — even a rater watches a recording of a system that included the first therapist. The disciplined move is to treat her interventions as experiments and read the circuit's response, including her place in it.
scenarios.hint: Her question changed the room. What if the symptom is the system's answer to her?
objectives: Include the observer in the system being analyzed
Reframe symptoms as circuit functions
evidence: Places the therapist inside the circuit and reads the symptom as systemic feedback

domains.name: Modern Systems Thinking
domains.description: Where cybernetics lives today: system dynamics, viable systems model, and complexity science.

scenarios.title: VSM Diagnosis: The Missing System 4
scenarios.situation: A 300-person logistics firm runs operations superbly (System 1) and coordinates daily work well (System 2), but strategic planning is just the CEO's gut feel, there is no market-intelligence function, and every 'strategy' is a reaction to the last crisis. Two agile competitors are eating its key accounts.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnose with Beer's Viable System Model. What is missing and what is the prescription?
choices: System 3 (control) is missing: add more management layers to tighten operational control

System 4 (intelligence) is missing: the firm has no outward- and future-looking function scanning the environment and modeling futures; prescribe a dedicated intelligence capacity feeding the policy level, closing the 3-4 homeostat between present operations and future adaptation
System 5 (policy/identity) is missing: the CEO should write a mission statement
Nothing is missing: gut-feel strategy worked for twenty years, so the competitors' gains are temporary
scenarios.why: In VSM, System 4 looks outward and forward — environment scanning, modeling, future planning — and holds the homeostatic tension with System 3 (present operations). A firm with strong S1/S2 but no S4 is viable today and blind tomorrow: it can only react. The prescription is an institutionalized intelligence function, not a mission statement or more control layers.
scenarios.hint: Which VSM system looks outward and forward? Who does that job here?
objectives: Identify VSM System 4 and its function
Diagnose its absence in an organization
evidence: Names missing System 4 and prescribes an intelligence function feeding policy

scenarios.title: Emergence at the Intersection
scenarios.situation: A city's new 'smart' intersection has perfect sensors, adaptive signals, and per-car optimization. Yet at rush hour a phantom jam forms with no accident, no bottleneck, no single cause — just stop-and-go waves. The vendor blames 'irrational drivers' and proposes stricter per-car control.
scenarios.prompt: What is the complexity-thinking diagnosis?
