The design principle: every automated loop needs damping proportional to its velocity — breakers, kill switches, speed bumps — built into the loop, because post-hoc human intervention cannot catch a loop that outruns human reaction time by six orders of magnitude.

example.code: May 6, 2010: Dow -998 points in ~20 minutes, then mostly recovered. Chain: large E-mini sell -> HFT momentum algorithms sell -> stop-losses trigger -> more selling -> liquidity vanishes as market-makers withdraw (their own risk loops) -> prices gap down absurdly (Accenture at $0.01) -> breakers finally trip -> humans catch up -> recovery. Post-crash reforms: limit-up/limit-down bands, single-stock circuit breakers — damping installed at machine timescale.
example.walkthrough: Draw the 2010 loop with timescales labeled on every arrow: milliseconds for algorithm arrows, minutes for human arrows. The diagram convicts the architecture by itself — no narrative needed.

pitfalls: Blaming the initial seller: triggers are interchangeable; the loop's gain is the story.
Concluding algorithms are ungovernable: they are governable by damping designed at their own timescale.
Assuming your domain is exempt: any automated decision loop faster than its oversight has a Flash Crash waiting.
lessons.try_it: Name the fastest automated loop in your organization (deploy pipeline, trading, bidding, scaling). What damps it, and at what timescale does the damping operate? If nothing does, design the breaker.

labs.title: Tune a thermostat, break a thermostat
labs.objective: Simulate a negative-feedback temperature controller and discover experimentally how sensor delay destroys stability.
steps: Copy the lesson's thermostat simulation into a file thermo.py.
Run it with delay=0 and record the final temperature — confirm it settles near the 20.0 target.
Re-run with delay=4, then delay=8, printing the last 10 readings each time; note when oscillation appears.
Add a bang-bang variant (full power below target, zero above) at delay=0 and compare its swing to proportional control.
Write two sentences: in a real deployment, what would you measure first — the control law or the loop delay? Why?

checks.hint: Print the delay value and final temperature on one line so the check can see the experiment ran.

labs.title: Measure the surprise
labs.objective: Compute Shannon entropy of a message source and build an optimal-ish variable-length code, proving Format B beats Format A.
steps: Define a source with four event types and probabilities, e.g., A=0.5, B=0.25, C=0.125, D=0.125.
Compute the entropy H = -sum(p * log2(p)) and the fixed-length cost (2 bits per event).
Assign codes by hand (A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111) and compute the average code length.
Verify your average length sits between the entropy and the fixed-length cost.
State in one line what the entropy value means operationally for this source.

checks.hint: Print the computed entropy with the word 'entropy' so the check can confirm the calculation ran.

labs.title: Build a Feedback Loop Simulation
labs.objective: Simulate a thermostat with gain and delay — then break it on purpose.
steps: Open the Terminal tab.
Observe: does the temperature converge, oscillate, or overshoot? Note the gain (1.5).
Raise the gain: change 1.5 to 4.0 and re-run — observe oscillation (delay + high gain).
State the control lesson in one sentence.

checks.hint: Run the thermostat simulation and observe convergence.
Confirm power output is printed per timestep.

labs.title: Compute Entropy by Hand (Then Verify)
labs.objective: Calculate the entropy of biased coins by hand, then verify computationally.
steps: Open the Terminal tab.
Type exactly: python3 -c "import math; h=lambda p: -(p*math.log2(p)+(1-p)*math.log2(1-p)); print('fair:',round(h(0.5),3)); print('70/30:',round(h(0.7),3)); print('99/1:',round(h(0.99),3))"
Record the three values. Which coin carries the most information per flip?
Explain: why does the 99/1 coin carry almost no information?
Connect: what does this say about 'data' vs 'information'?

checks.hint: Compute entropies and confirm fair coin = 1.0 bit.
Confirm the biased coin's low entropy.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — entropy is now a number you have computed, not a word you have read.

labs.title: Draw Three Loops
labs.objective: Diagram three feedback loops from your life with sensor/comparator/effector labeled.
steps: On paper:
Loop 1 (homeostasis): body temperature or hunger — label sensor, comparator, effector, sign.
Loop 2 (engineered): thermostat or cruise control — same labels.
Loop 3 (social): a habit loop or team dynamic — find the feedback, name its sign.
For each: what happens if the sensor lags? (Predict the oscillation.)

checks.hint: Confirm sensor identification.
Confirm loop diagrams.

labs.success_message: Lab complete — you now see loops everywhere. That is the cybernetic eye.

labs.title: Simulate Oscillation
labs.objective: Code a delayed feedback loop and watch it oscillate — then stabilize it.
steps: Open the Terminal tab.

Type exactly: python3 -c "t=20; hist=[20]*5
for i in range(30):
 err=22-hist[-5]; adj=max(-2,min(2,err*1.0)); t=max(0,t+adj-0.8); hist.append(t)
 print(f'step {i}: {t:.1f}')" | head -15
Observe: does it converge or oscillate? (Delay=5 steps causes hunting.)
Reduce gain (err*0.3) and re-run — observe stabilization.
State the lesson: gain × delay decides stability.

checks.hint: Run the delay simulation.
Confirm delay buffer usage.

labs.title: Concept Map Sprint
labs.objective: Map 12 cybernetics concepts with labeled relationships in 20 minutes.
steps: On paper:

labs.title: 300-Word Essay Sprint
labs.objective: Argue both sides of a cybernetic question in 300 words, timed.
steps: Set a 25-minute timer.
Prompt: 'Is a social media platform autopoietic?'
Structure: claim (100w) → counter (100w) → synthesis (100w).
Use at least 3 technical terms correctly (autopoiesis, feedback, observer).
Read aloud: does it argue or ramble? Revise once.

checks.hint: Confirm technical term usage.
Confirm both-sides structure.

labs.title: Map a Feedback Loop in Your Organization
labs.objective: Diagram one real reinforcing or balancing loop in your workplace, labeling every sensor, comparator, reference, effector, and delay.
steps: Choose a recurring pattern: a metric that keeps moving the wrong way, a chronic firefight, or a process that oscillates.
List the variables involved as nouns with direction (e.g., 'backlog size,' not 'backlog problems').
Draw the causal arrows between variables, marking each link + (same direction) or - (opposite direction).
Label the loop organs: which variable is sensed, what reference it is compared against, who/what acts as effector, and where the delays sit.
Determine the loop sign by counting - links (odd = balancing, even = reinforcing) and predict the loop's long-term behavior.
Propose one structural intervention: which single arrow would you rewire, and what would change?

checks.command: State the loop sign and the behavior it predicts
checks.output: e.g., 'Reinforcing: backlog grows exponentially because each delay increases future backlog'
checks.hint: Count the '-' links: odd = balancing, even = reinforcing.

checks.command: Name the weakest loop organ (sensor, comparator, reference, effector)
checks.output: e.g., 'Comparator: the target is ticket count, not resolution quality'
checks.hint: Ask which organ, if fixed, would change the loop's behavior most.

checks.command: Describe your one-arrow intervention
checks.output: e.g., 'Rewire the bonus from tickets-closed to reopen-rate; the reinforcing loop becomes balancing'
checks.hint: The best interventions rewire structure, not people.

labs.debrief: You turned a vague complaint into a testable loop diagram with named organs and a predicted behavior. Most organizational problems become solvable once drawn this way — the diagram is the diagnosis, and the rewired arrow is the prescription.

labs.title: PID Tuning Thought Experiment
labs.objective: Tune a hypothetical PID loop on paper, predicting the effect of each term change before 'applying' it.
steps: Set the scene: a water-tank level controller. The tank drains unpredictably (disturbance), a pump fills it (effector), a float sensor reads level with a 5-second lag.
Start with P-only control at moderate gain. Predict: what happens to steady-state error when the drain rate changes? What happens if you double the gain?
Add integral action. Predict: what happens to the steady-state error? What new risk appears (hint: the 5-second sensor lag)?
Add derivative action. Predict: how does it interact with the sensor lag and with measurement noise?
Introduce integral windup: the pump saturates at max while the level stays low. Predict the overshoot when the drain stops, then design the anti-windup fix.
Write your final tuning (P/I/D settings described qualitatively: low/medium/high) and justify each choice against the lag, the disturbance, and the saturation.

checks.command: Predict P-only behavior under changing drain
checks.output: 'Proportional leaves steady-state error that grows with drain rate; doubling gain halves error but risks oscillation via the 5s lag'
checks.hint: P corrects proportional to current error only — it cannot eliminate persistent error.

checks.command: Name the risk integral adds with a laggy sensor
checks.output: 'Overshoot and oscillation: the integrator keeps accumulating during the 5s blind period'
checks.hint: What does the integrator do while the sensor hasn't caught up?

checks.command: State your anti-windup design
checks.output: e.g., 'Freeze integration while the pump is saturated'
checks.hint: Windup is the integrator accumulating error it cannot act on.

labs.debrief: You reasoned through P, I, and D as distinct organs with distinct failure modes, and confronted the two classic PID pathologies — lag-induced oscillation and integral windup. Real tuning is this thought experiment plus patience: predict first, then touch the knobs.

labs.title: Calculate Channel Capacity
labs.objective: Compute Shannon entropy and Shannon-Hartley capacity for three realistic cases, and use the results to judge a vendor claim.
steps: Case A: a binary alarm that fires (1) 10% of the time and is silent (0) 90% of the time. Compute H = -(0.1*log2(0.1) + 0.9*log2(0.9)).
Case B: a 4-symbol sensor code with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125. Compute its entropy and compare with the 2 bits/symbol a fixed code would use.
Case C: a 20 kHz radio channel at 20 dB SNR (power ratio 100). Compute C = 20000 * log2(101).
A vendor claims their modem pushes 200 kbps through the Case C channel. Judge the claim against your computed capacity.
For Case A, design the ideal coding insight: how many bits per alarm reading does the source coding theorem say you need, and what does that imply for a year's worth of readings?
Write a two-sentence verdict a manager could understand: what the math allows, and what it forbids.

checks.command: Report Case A entropy
Report Case C capacity and the vendor verdict
checks.output: 'C ~= 133 kbps; the 200 kbps claim violates the Shannon limit'

checks.command: State the Case B compression opportunity
checks.output: 'H = 1.75 bits/symbol vs 2 fixed — ~12.5% compressible'

labs.debrief: You computed entropy as surprise-per-symbol and capacity as a hard physical ceiling, then used the ceiling to falsify an impossible claim. That is the whole practical power of Shannon: numbers that say 'no' to datasheets.

labs.title: Trace Information Flow
labs.objective: Audit how decision-relevant information actually travels through your team, and find where signal dies.
steps: Pick one recurring decision (e.g., weekly prioritization, incident response, release go/no-go).
Map the information path: who senses what, through which channel, to whom, with what delay — draw it as a chain.
For each link, estimate the signal-to-noise ratio: how much of what arrives is decision-relevant vs noise?
Apply Bateson's test to each report or dashboard on the path: did it change any decision in the last month? Mark the ones that failed.
Find the narrowest point: the link with the worst SNR or the longest delay — that is your channel bottleneck.
Propose one flow redesign: what gets cut, what gets a faster path, and what new signal the decision actually needs (requisite variety check).

checks.command: Name the decision and its current information path
checks.output: e.g., 'Release go/no-go: QA report -> Slack -> engineer skim -> gut-feel vote; 3-day delay'
checks.hint: Follow one real recent decision, not the documented process.

checks.command: List reports that failed Bateson's test
checks.output: e.g., 'The 40-metric dashboard: zero decisions changed in 6 weeks'
checks.hint: If no decision changed, it carried no information — regardless of bit count.

checks.command: State your one flow redesign
checks.output: e.g., 'Kill the dashboard; pipe the 3 decision metrics to the release channel with a 1-hour SLA'
checks.hint: Cut noise, shorten the path, match variety to the decision.

labs.debrief: You traced information as it actually flows — not as the org chart says — and applied both Shannon (SNR, delay, bottleneck) and Bateson (did it make a difference?). The redesign you proposed is an information-theoretic intervention, not just a process tweak.

labs.title: Run a VSM Diagnosis
labs.objective: Audit a real organization against Beer's five systems and deliver a viability verdict with triage order.
steps: Choose an organization you know well (your employer, a client, a volunteer group).
Identify S1: list the operational units that directly do the work and serve the environment.
Identify S2: find what coordinates the S1 units day-to-day (schedules, standards, shared protocols) — note oscillation where S2 is absent.
Identify S3/S3*: find who bargains resources and holds accountability (S3), and whether anyone audits reality directly, bypassing reports (S3*).
Identify S4 and S5: find the outward/future-scanning function (S4) and the identity-arbitration function (S5) — be brutal about whether they exist or are merely titled.
Deliver the verdict: viable / viable-with-gaps / non-viable, the missing functions, the failure each gap predicts, and the triage order with reasons.

checks.command: List S1 through S5 as found (or missing)
checks.output: e.g., 'S1 strong; S2 weak; S3 gut-feel; S3* absent; S4 absent; S5 nominal'
checks.hint: Functions, not departments — a titled 'strategy team' that only reacts is not S4.

checks.command: State the viability verdict and one predicted failure
checks.output: e.g., 'Viable today, blind tomorrow: missing S4 predicts strategic surprise within 18 months'
checks.hint: Each missing function predicts a specific failure mode.

checks.command: Give the triage order
checks.output: e.g., 'S5 identity first, then S3/S2, then S4 — because control needs a target before intelligence matters'
checks.hint: Order by dependency: what must exist before the next fix can aim at anything?

labs.debrief: You performed Beer's viability audit: functions instead of boxes, recursion-aware, verdict-first. The triage order is the real skill — viability is not a score, it is a sequence of repairs ordered by what depends on what.

labs.title: Build a Causal Loop Diagram
labs.objective: Construct a multi-loop causal diagram of a complex problem, finding at least one reinforcing and one balancing loop plus a delay.
steps: Choose a persistent problem: customer churn, technical debt growth, burnout cycles, or traffic congestion.
Brainstorm 8-12 variables as measurable nouns (e.g., 'overtime hours,' 'defect rate') — no vague nouns like 'problems.'
Connect variables with causal arrows, labeling each + or - and noting the evidence or reasoning for each link.
Find closed loops: trace around until you return to the start. Identify at least one reinforcing (even number of - links) and one balancing loop (odd number).
Mark every significant delay with a double-hash on the arrow, and note which loop dominates under current conditions.
Write the story the diagram tells in three sentences, then name the highest-leverage intervention (Meadows: prefer goals and loop structure over parameters).

checks.command: Name one reinforcing and one balancing loop from your diagram
checks.output: e.g., 'R: overtime -> fatigue -> defects -> rework -> more overtime; B: overtime -> hiring pressure -> new staff -> less overtime (delayed)'
checks.hint: Trace closed paths; count the '-' links on each.

checks.command: Mark the dominant loop and the key delay
checks.output: e.g., 'R dominates: the hiring delay (6 months) lets the burnout loop run unchecked'
checks.hint: The loop with the shortest delay usually dominates early.

checks.command: State the highest-leverage intervention
checks.output: e.g., 'Cap overtime (loop structure) rather than wellness posters (parameter)'
checks.hint: Meadows: change the loop or the goal, not the poster.

labs.debrief: You built a genuine multi-loop model with delays and dominance — the core artifact of systems thinking. The three-sentence story is the test: if the diagram cannot be narrated, it is decoration; if it can, it is a decision tool.

labs.title: Design a Negative Feedback Intervention
labs.objective: Design a complete autoscaling policy as a control loop: sensor, comparator, effector, delays, damping, and feedforward.
steps: Define the controlled variable and its reference: what exactly are you holding stable (e.g., p99 latency < 300ms, or CPU ~60%)? Write the setpoint explicitly.
Design the sensor: what metric, sampled how often, smoothed over what window — and what is the measurement delay?
Design the comparator: scale-up and scale-down thresholds with a deadband (hysteresis) between them; justify the deadband width against the warmup delay.
Design the effector and its limits: step size per action, cooldown periods matched to the warmup delay, min/max instance bounds.
Add feedforward: what predictable disturbances (deploy schedules, marketing events, cron jobs) can you scale for before they hit?
Stress-test on paper: a 10x traffic spike in 2 minutes with an 8-minute warmup — trace what your loop does minute by minute and find where it still oscillates or saturates.

checks.command: State sensor, comparator, and effector with numbers
checks.output: e.g., 'Sensor: p99 latency, 1-min avg; comparator: scale up >400ms, down <150ms; effector: +2/-1 instances, 10-min cooldown'
checks.hint: Every organ needs numbers: sample window, thresholds, step sizes, cooldowns.

checks.command: Justify the deadband and cooldown against the warmup delay
checks.output: e.g., 'Cooldown 10 min > 8-min warmup so in-flight capacity is counted before the next decision'
checks.hint: Corrections must wait for prior corrections to take effect.

checks.command: Describe the 10x-spike trace outcome
checks.output: e.g., 'Feedforward pre-scales from the event calendar; feedback handles the residual; saturation at max bound triggers the page'
checks.hint: No loop handles everything — name what saturates and what happens then.

labs.debrief: You designed autoscaling as control theory, not as config YAML: explicit setpoint, deadband against delay, cooldowns respecting actuation lag, and feedforward for the predictable. The paper stress-test is the difference between a policy and a hope.

labs.title: Audit an ML Training Loop
labs.objective: Audit a model training setup as nested feedback loops and write the ship/no-ship decision rule.
steps: Draw the inner loop: gradient descent minimizing training loss — label the error signal, the gain (learning rate), and the actuator (weight updates).
Draw the outer loop: validation monitoring generalization — label its error signal (val loss / val metric) and its actuators (early stopping, regularization, data changes).
Define divergence criteria: exactly what pattern in the two curves means 'memorizing, not learning'?
Write the ship rule: the precise conditions under which the outer loop permits deployment (e.g., 'val metric within 2% of best for 3 evals, train-val gap < 5%').
Add the production loop: what post-deployment signal (drift detection, live accuracy sampling) continues the outer loop after shipping, and what triggers rollback or retraining?
Red-team your rule: describe a scenario where all your gates pass but the model still fails in production — what loop is missing?

checks.command: State the inner and outer loop error signals
checks.output: 'Inner: training loss gradient; outer: validation loss/metric trend'
checks.hint: Each loop needs its own error signal and its own actuator.

checks.command: Write the ship rule precisely
checks.output: e.g., 'Ship iff val metric >= best-2% for 3 consecutive evals AND train-val gap < 5%'
checks.hint: A rule you cannot evaluate mechanically is not a rule.

checks.command: Name the red-team failure mode
checks.output: e.g., 'Training-serving skew: validation data no longer matches production distribution'
checks.hint: The outer loop is only as good as its sensor — validation data.

labs.debrief: You separated the loop that optimizes from the loop that judges, wrote a mechanical ship rule, and extended the loop into production. The red-team step is the cybernetic habit: every loop has a sensor blind spot — name it before reality does.

labs.title: Dissect a Historical Failure
labs.objective: Apply the five-lens case method to Three Mile Island and produce a one-page autopsy.
steps: Lens 1 — anatomy: list TMI's sensors, comparators, references, and effectors in the control room; mark which reported commands vs states.
Lens 2 — loops: identify the physical positive-feedback risk (core heat vs coolant) and the operators' balancing intent; show how false feedback inverted the intended correction.
Lens 3 — delay/timescale: note the 2+ hour duration of the stuck-open valve vs the operators' mental model of a transient event.
Lens 4 — variety: count the disturbance (a novel plant state) against the operators' trained response repertoire; find the gap.
Lens 5 — observer: describe the operators' information state minute by minute vs the physical state; show where false feedback made the wrong action reasonable.
Write the one-page autopsy: verdict, the single most important architectural fix, and one lesson that transfers to your own field.

checks.command: Name the command-vs-state sensor confusion
checks.output: 'Valve light reported solenoid command, not stem position; pressurizer level reported bubble-distorted level, not inventory'
checks.hint: Two instruments, two lies — find both.

checks.command: State the architectural fix
checks.output: 'Sensors must report physical state; add diverse, independent sensing on safety-critical variables'
checks.hint: Fix the loop, not the operators.

checks.command: Transfer one lesson to your field
checks.output: e.g., 'Our deploy dashboard shows "restart sent," not "service healthy" — same confusion'
checks.hint: The pattern generalizes; find your instance.

labs.debrief: You ran a full five-lens autopsy and extracted a transferable design rule. The discipline — reconstructing the actors' information state rather than judging from hindsight — is what makes case study a method instead of a story.

labs.title: Compare Two Cases: Toyota vs Three Mile Island
labs.objective: Contrast a feedback success (Toyota's andon) with a feedback failure (TMI) on shared axes to extract portable design principles.
steps: Set the comparative axes: (1) sensor truthfulness, (2) feedback delay, (3) effector authority, (4) operator mental models, (5) response to the unexpected.
Score TMI on each axis in one sentence per axis, citing the case facts.
Score Toyota's andon system on each axis in one sentence per axis, citing the case facts.
Identify the axis where the two cases differ most sharply, and explain why that axis dominates the outcomes.
Synthesize: write three portable design principles that hold across both cases (e.g., 'Feedback must report state, not intention').
Apply: take one principle and sketch how you would implement it in a system you work with this month.

checks.command: State the sharpest axis of difference
checks.output: e.g., 'Sensor truthfulness: andon senses the actual defect; TMI's light sensed the command'
checks.hint: Which single axis, if swapped, would most change each outcome?

checks.command: List your three portable principles
checks.output: e.g., '1. Sense state, not commands. 2. Shorten delay before adding authority. 3. Train models of physics, not just procedures.'
checks.hint: Principles must survive translation to a different domain.

checks.command: Sketch one implementation for your own system
checks.output: e.g., 'Replace deploy "success" messages with health-check-verified state before marking green'
checks.hint: Concrete, this month, one system.

labs.debrief: Comparison on shared axes turned two stories into engineering principles. The andon/TMI pair is ideal because they are near-mirror images: same loop anatomy, opposite truthfulness — which is why the principles you extracted will travel.

labs.title: Identify Goodhart Cases
labs.objective: Hunt down three live Goodhart/Campbell effects in your environment and redesign one metric to resist corruption.
steps: List five metrics you are judged by (or that judge others): KPIs, OKRs, ratings, scores, counts.
For each, ask: if someone optimized this metric ruthlessly while harming the underlying goal, what would they do? Write the gaming strategy explicitly.
Score each metric 1-5 on corruptibility: how easily does the gaming strategy succeed, and how invisible is it?
Pick the most corruptible metric. Diagnose the loop: what is the measure, what is the goal, and where does the measure diverge from the goal?
Redesign it using Goodhart resistance: pair it with a counter-metric, rotate or randomize measurement, measure outcomes not activities, or return judgment to informed human review.
Write the before/after: the old metric, its gaming strategy, and why your redesign is harder to game without doing the real work.

checks.command: Name three metrics and their gaming strategies
checks.output: e.g., 'Tickets closed -> close with shallow fixes; lines of code -> verbose code; NPS -> beg for 10s'
checks.hint: Be the adversary: how would you cheat each metric while looking good?

checks.command: Diagnose the worst one: measure vs goal divergence
checks.output: e.g., 'AHT measures speed; the goal is resolution — they diverge on complex calls'
checks.hint: The divergence point is where the redesign must aim.

checks.command: State the redesigned metric and its resistance logic
checks.output: e.g., 'Replace AHT with resolution-rate + sampled call review; gaming requires actually resolving'
checks.hint: A good redesign makes cheating equivalent to doing the job.

labs.debrief: You learned to see metrics as adversarial interfaces: every number you publish is an optimization target for someone. The redesign skill — making the metric hard to game without doing the work — is second-order cybernetics applied to management.

labs.title: Model a Black Box
labs.objective: Build a behavioral model of an opaque system using only controlled input variation, and state the model's limits honestly.
steps: Choose a black box: a vendor API, a colleague's approval process, a smart appliance, a recommendation feed — anything whose internals you cannot see.
Enumerate the inputs you can manipulate and the outputs you can observe. Fix all inputs but one.
Vary that input across at least 5 distinct values, recording the output each time in a table. Repeat for a second input.
Look for the transfer pattern: thresholds, proportional regions, saturation, delays, hysteresis — describe it in plain language plus a sketch.
Make one prediction about an untested input combination, then test it. Record whether the model held.

Write the model's charter of limits: the input ranges tested, the conditions not tested, and where you expect the model to break (second-order honesty: your probing may have changed the box, e.g., rate limits, learning effects).

checks.command: Present your input-output table (5+ values, two inputs)
checks.output: e.g., 'API latency vs payload size: 1KB->80ms, 10KB->95ms, 100KB->400ms, 1MB->timeout...'
checks.hint: One input at a time; everything else fixed.

checks.command: State your prediction and the test result
checks.output: e.g., 'Predicted timeout above 500KB; tested 750KB -> timeout confirmed'
checks.hint: A model that cannot predict is a diary, not a model.

checks.command: Write two limits of your model
checks.output: e.g., 'Untested under concurrent load; my probing may have triggered rate limiting, changing the box'
checks.hint: The observer clause: did your experiment perturb the system?

labs.debrief: You did Ashby's black-box method end to end: controlled variation, transfer pattern, prediction, and an honest charter of limits including your own observer effect. That last clause is what separates cybernetic modeling from curve-fitting.

simulations.title: The autoscaler that fed on its own alerts
simulations.brief: At 03:00 the fleet scaled from 12 to 400 instances, then collapsed. The scaling signal came from the monitoring the scaler itself was saturating. Diagnose the loop.

steps.symptom: 03:00 scale-up triggered by p99 latency alert. Each new instance increased monitoring load, which raised reported latency, which triggered more scale-up.
options: Runaway positive feedback: the controller's actions amplified the sensor reading that drove the controller
A DDoS attack
Bad deploy at 03:00
The monitoring agent has a memory leak
evidence: metrics.txt
03:00 p99=900ms (12 instances) -> 03:20 p99=2400ms (180 instances) -> 03:40 fleet 400, API down. Monitoring scrape load per instance: constant. Total scrape load grew 33x.
scaler-config.txt
Scale rule: IF p99 > 800ms THEN add 20%. Cooldown: 0s. No damping, no max cap.
steps.explain: This is circular causality in production: the effector (new instances) fed the sensor (latency, inflated by scrape load), which re-triggered the controller. Wiener's warning made concrete — a control loop with no damping and a corrupted sensor diverges.

steps.symptom: Positive feedback confirmed. What breaks the loop?
options: Add more instances faster
Introduce negative feedback: cooldown periods, a max instance cap, damping on the scale signal, and a sensor that measures real user latency instead of scrape-loaded latency
Disable the autoscaler permanently
Increase the latency threshold to 5000ms
evidence: control-theory.txt
Stability requires negative feedback: the correction must oppose the error, with delay and gain tuned so the loop converges instead of oscillating or diverging.
steps.explain: You do not fix a control loop by pushing harder — you fix it by making the feedback negative and honest: cooldowns and caps bound the gain, and an uncorrupted sensor closes the loop on reality.

simulations.debrief: Every autoscaler, alert pipeline, and incident response is a control loop. Ask of each one: what is the sensor, what is the effector, is the feedback negative, and what happens at the extremes. Positive feedback always finds the extreme.

simulations.title: Design the detection-response feedback loop
simulations.brief: You are designing the SOC's core loop: detection -> triage -> containment -> learning. The CISO asks where automation belongs and where humans belong. Decide the control architecture.

steps.symptom: Proposal A: full automation — detect, isolate, remediate, close, no humans. Proposal B: your design.
options: Proposal A — speed wins, humans are the bottleneck
A layered loop: fast inner loop (automated containment on high-confidence, reversible actions) inside a slow outer loop (human review, rule tuning, lessons learned feeding back into detection)
No automation — analysts handle everything
Automate only the ticketing
evidence: incident-review.txt
Last quarter: 2 false-positive auto-isolations took down payroll. 1 slow human triage let ransomware dwell 6 hours. Both failure modes are loop-design failures.
wiener-note.txt
Control without communication fails; communication without control is noise. The loop needs both machine speed and human judgment, each where it belongs.
steps.explain: Cybernetics gives the answer structure: nested loops at different timescales. The fast loop handles what is reversible and high-confidence; the slow loop — humans — handles judgment, novelty, and tuning the fast loop itself. Either extreme fails exactly as the incident review shows.

steps.symptom: The layered loop is approved. Where does the learning feedback go — what does the outer loop actually change?
options: It writes the incident report
It tunes the inner loop: detection thresholds, containment playbooks, confidence scores — every incident updates the controller's parameters
It hires more analysts
It buys more tools
evidence: soc-metrics.txt
MTTR fell 40% after the outer loop started feeding false-positive analysis back into rule tuning. Same tools, better controller.
steps.explain: The outer loop's product is a better inner loop. An incident that does not change a threshold, a playbook, or a score is information that never became control — entropy the organization paid for and threw away.

simulations.debrief: A SOC is a control system regulating the organization's risk state. Design it as nested feedback loops: fast automated inner loops for the reversible and certain, slow human outer loops for judgment — and every incident must tune the machine.

simulations.title: The deploy pipeline that could not decide
simulations.brief: The canary deployer has rolled forward and back six times in an hour. Each rollback triggers a redeploy, each redeploy triggers a rollback. Find the oscillation source.

steps.symptom: 18:00 deploy v2.4 -> 18:07 rollback (error budget) -> 18:12 redeploy (metrics recovered) -> 18:19 rollback... six cycles. Error rate hovers exactly at the threshold.
options: Hunting oscillation from delayed feedback: the health sensor lags reality, so the controller corrects for a state that no longer exists
The new version is simply broken
The old version is simply broken
Two engineers fighting over the deploy button
evidence: deployer.log
18:07 rollback decision used metrics from 17:52 (15-min aggregation lag). 18:12 redeploy used metrics from 18:00 (pre-rollback window). Each decision corrected the previous window's state.
metrics-raw.txt
Actual error rate: stable 0.8%, under the 1% threshold, the entire hour. The controller never saw the present.
steps.explain: Delayed feedback turns negative feedback into oscillation: by the time the sensor reports, the system has moved on, so every correction overshoots. The error rate was fine — the controller was steering by a stale map.

steps.symptom: Stale sensor confirmed. What stabilizes the loop?
options: Deploy faster to outrun the lag
Faster sensing plus hysteresis: shorten the aggregation window, and require the signal to clear the threshold by a margin for a sustained period before reversing a decision
Remove the error-budget gate
Increase the rollback threshold
evidence: control-theory.txt
Two cures for delay-induced oscillation: reduce the delay (faster sensor), and add hysteresis/deadband so the controller does not reverse on noise.
steps.explain: Hysteresis is the thermostat principle: the heater does not flip at exactly 20.0 degrees or it chatters forever. A margin plus a dwell time lets the loop settle instead of hunting.

simulations.debrief: Oscillation is the signature of feedback delay. When a system hunts — flapping between states — check the sensor's freshness before blaming the thing being controlled. Faster truth plus hysteresis calms the loop.

simulations.title: The SOC drowned in its own signals
simulations.brief: Alert volume tripled after a new log source came online: 12,000 alerts/day, 3 analysts. True positives are being missed in the flood. The channel is over capacity. Respond.

steps.symptom: 12,000 alerts/day. Analyst capacity: ~150 investigations/day. Missed: a real credential-stuffing campaign buried at position 9,400.
options: Hire 80 analysts
Treat it as a channel-capacity problem: the signal rate exceeds the receiver's bandwidth, so compress before transmitting — aggregate, deduplicate, prioritize, suppress the known-benign
Turn off the new log source
Tell analysts to work faster
evidence: alert-stats.txt
Of 12,000 daily alerts: 61% duplicates, 22% known-benign (tuned but not suppressed), 9% informational, 8% actionable. Effective signal: ~960/day.
shannon-note.txt
Information theory: a channel has finite capacity. When the source exceeds it, you encode smarter (compression, prioritization) — you cannot will the channel wider.
steps.explain: Shannon's answer applies to SOCs: the analysts are a finite-capacity channel. 92% of the volume is redundancy and noise — compress it out before it reaches the human, and the real signal fits the channel.

steps.symptom: Compression plan approved. What is the correct order of operations?
options: Suppress everything and tune later
Deduplicate first (safe, mechanical), then suppress the known-benign with documented rules, then risk-prioritize the remainder — measuring miss rate at each step
Prioritize first, dedupe later
Buy a bigger SIEM
evidence: rollout.txt
Dedup: -61% volume, zero miss risk. Known-benign suppression: -22%, each rule peer-reviewed. Prioritization: ranked queue, miss rate monitored weekly.
steps.explain: Order by reversibility and risk: mechanical dedup cannot hide signal, documented suppression is auditable, and prioritization keeps the residual risk visible and measured instead of silent.

simulations.debrief: Alert fatigue is an information-theoretic failure, not a morale failure. The fix is encoding: compress redundancy, filter the known-benign, prioritize the rest — and measure what the channel carries, not just its volume.

simulations.title: Hold the line: homeostasis under attack
simulations.brief: A traffic flood is pushing the API toward its breaking point. You must hold service levels steady — homeostasis — while the attack continues. Choose the control strategy.

steps.symptom: Traffic 8x normal, 70% from 200 source IPs with bot signatures. p99 latency climbing, error rate 2% and rising. SLO: 99.9% success.
options: Overprovision: spin up 10x capacity and absorb it
Negative-feedback control: rate-limit the abusive sources, shed low-priority load, serve degraded-but-correct responses — regulate the internal state against the disturbance
Shut down the API until the attack ends
Block the entire internet except allowlisted customers
evidence: capacity.txt
10x overprovisioning: 40 min to provision, cost 12x, and the botnet can scale faster than we can buy.
physio-note.txt
Homeostasis: the organism does not grow ten hearts under stress — it constricts vessels, prioritizes the brain, sheds heat. Regulate, don't just absorb.
steps.explain: Absorption loses to any attacker who can scale; shutdown surrenders. Homeostatic control — sense the disturbance, oppose it proportionally, protect the essential functions — holds the SLO while the storm passes.

steps.symptom: Rate limiting is holding the SLO. The attack shifts: now low-and-slow from 50,000 residential IPs. Your controller's move?
options: Give up — it cannot be rate-limited by IP anymore
Adapt the controller: shift from IP-based to behavior-based signals (request patterns, TLS fingerprints, challenge-response), keeping the same homeostatic goal
Block all residential IPs
Raise the rate limits so legitimate users are unaffected
evidence: adaptation.txt
Second-order control: when the disturbance changes form, the controller must change its sensor, not its goal. Goal (SLO) is invariant; the means adapt.
steps.explain: This is the cybernetic lesson in one move: the goal stays fixed while the control strategy adapts to the disturbance. Rigid controllers break; adaptive controllers hold.

simulations.debrief: Homeostasis is the original control problem: hold the essential variable steady while the environment rages. Sense honestly, oppose proportionally, and when the attack changes shape, change the sensor — never the goal.

Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.

A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.

ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.

Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.

Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.

Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
